title: About me
text:
Hi, I’m Ana, a Mexican currently at Madagascar —for now—. I’m a woman of many passions, led by creativity, logic, and the joy of transformation.
Here I share my CV :  CV 
But, to get to know me better, here are my other passions :

Data analysisBio & techContinous LearningHobbies


Curiosity didn’t kill the cat—for me, exploring is a necessity. I love seeing how digging into data can turn into knowledge, clearer decisions, and better understanding.
My expertise lies in programming, statistics, and data reproducibility, which I’ve practiced across international projects, from genomics to image analysis. I’ve developed skills in multiple programming languages (R, Python, SQL) and visualization tools (Tableau, Shiny, Quarto) and I love data challenges.


With a degree in Biotechnology and a Master’s in Plant Breeding, my most recent projects have been linked to agriculture and, more broadly, to innovation and technology.
Advances in tech can be both inspiring and risky, which is why I enjoy staying informed, learning how to make better use of technologies, reflecting on ethics, and exploring how we can move forward together.


I love learning—both in science and in life. From languages (I speak Spanish, English, French, Italian, and now a bit of Malagasy) to geography.
I also love exploring new cultures and places, that’s what brought me to Mada in the 1st place.


My hobbies include dancing, painting, sports, and reading. I enjoy challenging myself with new things, right now it’s volleyball and diving.

title: R training at dP SPAD
text:
Stats without stress? Oh yes, it’s a match… and we are still going!
From April 13th to 17th, the dP SPAD (Research and Training Platform in Partnership “High-Altitude Production Systems and Sustainability”) in Ambatobe, Madagascar, hosted an intensive week on R, RStudio, and data analysis. But wait, we didn’t stop there!
This wasn’t just a one-week workshop; it is an ongoing learning journey. One month later, the adventure continues with 10 brilliant PhD students from dP SPAD, CIRAD (French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development), and their partners.
Through online follow-ups and personalized 1-on-1 mentoring, we are breaking down every function and fine-tuning every script to fit their exact research data.
Because let’s be honest: programming in R and statistics shouldn’t be so stressful. They are here to make your data speak beautifully!
Kudos to these amazing researchers for their hard work and dedication.

title: 6 Common R Errors and How to Fix Them
text:
I remember when I was just starting out with R, I was very excited and hyped but the errors in my code were so frequent that I almost gave up learning. Sometimes, I even preferred to continue in Excel knowing it will take me many more hours than just solve my code!
If that sounds familiar, you’re not alone. Most R errors come down to a handful of recurring issues.
Here are 6 of the most common ones and ofc how to avoid them.


1. Start With Well-Formatted Data
Before you write a single line of code, make sure your data is structured properly. Messy column names, merged cells, inconsistent formats, or mixed data types in a single column are a recipe for hours of debugging later. A clean, tidy dataset from the start will save you far more time than it costs you upfront.
Try to follow these rules :

one row = one statistical invidual - personne, objetc of study
one column = one variable = one information
not joint cells! from excel… please!



2. Watch Your Naming — and What You’ve Actually Run
Misspelling a function, variable, dataset, or package name is one of the most common (and most overlooked) sources of errors.
If you’re sure you spelled everything correctly but you still get “object ‘…’ not found”, check one thing first: did you actually run the code that defines it?
Here’s the key thing to remember: writing code in an R script doesn’t mean it’s been executed. Unlike the console, a script only runs when you actually click Run (or use the keyboard shortcut). Until then, R has no idea that object exists.







3. Write Your Code in a Script, Not the Console
Typing code directly into the console can feel quick and tempting, especially for one-off checks. But it’s not a great habit for real work, anything you run there isn’t saved.
A better approach: write your code in an R Script. Run it from there, and you’ll be able to save your work, rerun it later, and share it with others (including future-you, who will thank present-you).


4. Check for Missing Parentheses, Brackets, or Quotes
A tiny typo can bring your whole script to a halt. One of the most common culprits: a missing closing parenthesis ), curly brace }, square bracket ], or quotation mark. So sorry but you need to focus to detect them, normally R tries to give you a heads up, but you need to focus!


5. Learn to Read R’s Error Messages
R’s error messages can feel cryptic at first, but most of them are trying to tell you something very specific. Here’s a quick guide to the ones you’ll run into most often:

"could not find function '...'": Usually means the package isn’t loaded, or you’ve misspelled the function name. For example, typing boxsplot() instead of boxplot() will trigger exactly this error.
"object not found": The object you’re referencing doesn’t exist yet, or is empty. See tip #2.
"cannot open the connection": This usually means one of two things: R can’t find the file (often a typo in the file path), or a package failed to load because a system dependency is missing.
"non-numeric argument to a binary operator": You’re mixing data types in a calculation, like trying to do math with a number and a character value.

One more thing to keep in mind: R is case-sensitive. Data and data are two different objects to R — a small detail that causes a surprising number of headaches.


6. Keep Your Working Directory Organized



Please do not have your desktop organized as the one on the left!


A messy working directory makes everything harder: finding files, sourcing scripts, loading data. Take the time to organize your project folder from the start — separate folders for raw data, scripts, and outputs go a long way toward avoiding “cannot open the connection” errors down the line.

Debugging is a normal part of learning R and even experienced users run into these errors regularly. The difference is knowing how to read the message and where to look.
At the end, practice is what you need to master all these ! So do not worry! The more you write your script the more you’ll learn from it!

title: Writing for Botany One!
text:
I’m so excited to share this: I’ve joined Botany One as a contributing writer! 🌿
Botany One is non profit plant magazine, a weblog produced by The Annals of Botany Company, that has a mission to share and increase the understanding of plant biology.
If you know me, you know I’ve always had a deep love for science communication, my dream is to make research accessible, human, and genuinely exciting to read, not just for scientists, but for anyone curious about the world.
Through this new adventure, I’ll be interviewing scientists whose research inspires me — some of them close friends, others researchers whose work I’ve admired from afar — and sharing their stories around plant science, a field that motivates me deeply.
Because science belongs to everyone, and the more we talk about it, the further it goes. 🌱

title: Data Viz: 5 Tips to Make Your Charts Talk
text:
You know your data inside out. You’ve been staring at it for weeks, maybe months. So when you build a chart, the message feels obvious to you.
But here’s the catch: your audience hasn’t lived with your data like you have. What’s crystal clear to you as the expert can be completely confusing to them.
Good data visualization isn’t about showing everything you found, it’s about simplifying and telling a story your audience can actually follow. Here are 5 tips to get there.

1. Know the Difference: Exploratory vs. Explanatory Charts
Let’s dig into this first, because it changes everything else.
Exploratory charts are for you. They help you see first patterns and trends in your data — outliers, errors, unit mismatches, distributions. Think histograms, boxplots, scatterplots. Messy, quick, informative. Nobody else needs to see these.
Explanatory charts are for your audience. These are the ones you polish and publish — in a report, a presentation, a paper. Their only job is to make a point and lead your audience straight to the takeaway. If you skip this distinction, you risk showing raw exploratory charts to people who don’t have the context to read them — and you waste everyone’s time, including your own.
👉 Rule of thumb: if it’s exploratory, keep it messy and fast. If it’s explanatory, make every element earn its place and use strong, confident language around it.







2. Clarify Your Message First
Before you even open your plotting library, ask yourself:

What do these variables actually represent, in plain terms?
Who is my audience, and what do they already know?
What do I want my audience to react to? Which takeaway?

Once you know your message, use your chart to reinforce it: add target lines, reference lines, or annotations that point straight at your takeaway. Just don’t overdo it — an annotation on every data point defeats the purpose.


3. Choose the Right Chart for the Job
Not every finding needs a chart. Sometimes a single number, a short sentence, or a simple table communicates faster — a percentage on its own can be more impactful than a graph around it.
When you do need a chart, let your goal decide the type:

Comparing categories (bigger vs. smaller): vertical bar charts work well for a few categories; order them ascending or descending when it helps the story.
Comparing many categories, or categories without a natural order: horizontal bar charts scale better and stay readable.
Showing change over time (growth, decline, trends): line charts are the go-to.
Showing parts of a whole: stacked bars work well, especially across categories or time.
Showing a single proportion (this part vs. the rest): pie charts — yes, the famous, often-criticized pie chart. They get a bad reputation because comparing slice sizes isn’t very objective, and they fall apart with more than 5–6 slices. But for one proportion, clearly labeled, they can still do the job.



4. Simplify, Simplify, Simplify
Overcomplication is the fastest way to lose your audience. Watch out for:

Too many lines on one chart
Too many colors
3D effects — they distort perception and make comparison genuinely harder. Avoid them, always.

Ask yourself: what does each element actually contribute? If the answer is “nothing,” cut it.
Practical habits:

Keep only the labels your audience actually needs.
Remove gridlines and background noise you don’t need — simplify what’s behind your data, not just the data itself.
Start your axis at 0 — unless you have a specific, well-justified reason to zoom in (e.g., highlighting a sharp change starting at a specific point).
Use labels intelligently — they should clarify, not clutter.



5. Use Color With Intention
Color is one of your most powerful tools — and one of the most misused. Skip the rainbow palette and your personal favorites. Instead, use color strategically to highlight your insight, not to decorate your chart.
A few principles:

Think about contrast — your key data point should visually stand out.
Be mindful of context: red often reads as “danger” or “alert,” so use it deliberately, not by default. Neutral tones like gray, black, or blue are often safer as your base palette.
Whatever you choose, stay consistent — the same category should always get the same color throughout your report or dashboard.

title: Telling Forest Stories with Tableau
text:
Exploring Data Storytelling, I chose to work with data from Madagascar—the country where I currently live. One of the most alarming environmental issues here is deforestation, which is not just a matter of numbers but a threat to biodiversity, communities, and the future of the island.
As part of a Tableau course (available at Coursera, there is a lot of options there actually…), I built interactive dashboards to visualize tree cover loss across time and regions.

The goal: raise awareness of Madagascar’s dramatic forest loss.
This project showed me how data visualization can tell stories that move beyond statistics—inviting reflection, and hopefully, inspiring action.

title: From Pixels to Guavas
text:
Freelance projects sometimes push you into new worlds—mine brought me to computer vision.
With a fruit producer company in Mexico, I have been working on building an image analysis pipeline in Python for a guava breeding program.

The challenge: create an automated system to measure, analyze, and classify different guava traits.

Along the way, I discovered tools I’d never heard of before as PlantCV (open-source image analysis software package, specifically for plant science) and I have been increasing my abilities in Python.
It’s been a winding road, but one that taught me how versatile data can be when combined with image analysis and -of course - creativity.

title: Stats training with APDRA
text:
We’re wrapping up the year with a project that was both challenging, motivating, and truly rewarding. My first training as the coach (hopefully, the first one from many others to come).
It was a statistics training called Stats sans stress, because statistics are not meant to stress us out — they’re meant to help us make sense of data.
The training took place in Antsirabe, Madagascar, with technical evaluation officers from APDRA (Association Pisciculture et Développement Rural in Africa).
We worked on data management and cleaning, as well as the foundations of essential statistical tests, always tailored to the group’s real needs. We explored lots of fish-related data 🐟 and dove into this fascinating world to turn numbers into clear, meaningful stories backed by solid statistics.
Because data do tell stories — and learning how to read them can be both useful and fun.
If you’d like to learn how to work with data in a clear, useful, and stress-free way with your team, feel free to get in touch.
